newsitem.title: UK: BT set to demand changes in MCI strategy.
newsitem.headline: BT set to demand changes in MCI strategy.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc is likely to tighten cost and management control at MCI Communications if their merger goes ahead on current terms, analysts said on Tuesday.
Shares in BT slipped 4.5p to 377p, moving against a rising market, following a report in the Financial Times that BT was not seeking to renegotiate terms of the $20 billion plus trans-Atlantic deal.

BT declined comment on the report, repeating that it hoped to complete a review of the deal by the end of August. The review was sparked after MCI surprised BT by forecasting losses of $800 million this year because of delays in breaking into U.S. local telephone markets.

The BT board is expected to meet on Thursday and the fate of the merger is almost certain to figure on the agenda. The stakes are high. The merged company, Concert Plc, would have annual revenues of more than $40 billion and 43 million customers.
Some reports have suggested that BT chairman Sir Iain Vallance and chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield could come under pressure if the deal fails to win over large institutional investors.

The Financial Times noted a filing by MCI to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission made no reference to any change in merger terms and took this as an indication that the deal would proceed as planned.
However, some London-based share analysts questioned whether too much had been read into the filing.

"It may be that terms will remain unchanged but I don't think the absence of a statement in the filing either confirms or undermines the supposition," said James Golob of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. He said the companies would "need their heads examining" to make a statement before BT had completed its review.

Golob said that a "face saving compromise" acceptable to both sides was likely to emerge. He said that the simplest way to reduce dilution for BT was to renegotiate the deal but added that legal obstacles may prevent this.

Other options included cutting costs by phasing start-up costs in local U.S. operations over a longer period or restructuring MCI's long-distance business in the U.S., where it is the second largest carrier.
James Ross, telecoms analyst with ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, said no-one could claim to second guess BT's plans with any accuracy.
"If you look at the probabilities, the odds are that you will not get a settlement that BT's shareholders are 100 percent happy with," he said.

Ross said BT may scale back MCI's local investment and take a stronger grip on its management to sell the deal to shareholders unhappy with the price it is paying for the 80 percent of MCI it does not control.

His view was shared by Credit Lyonnais Laing analyst Steve Scruton. "They will probably try and cut back on investment in the local loop which is the part of the business causing most problems," he said.
Scruton stated his misgivings about the deal.
"MCI was wrong to go aggressively into the local market and BT was wrong to overbid for MCI," he said, noting, however, that he believed BT remained determined that the deal should go ahead.
